purpose: Eribulin is a chemotherapy medicine used to treat certain types of breast cancer that have spread or come back after other treatments. It is also used to treat a type of soft tissue cancer called liposarcoma. Your doctor prescribes it when other cancer medicines have already been tried.
how_it_works: Cancer cells grow by dividing and multiplying rapidly. Eribulin works by interfering with tiny structures inside cancer cells called microtubules, which the cells need to split and copy themselves. By blocking these structures, eribulin stops cancer cells from dividing and causes them to die.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects include low white blood cell counts (which raises your infection risk), tiredness and weakness, hair loss, nausea, constipation, numbness or tingling in your hands and feet, joint or muscle pain, and loss of appetite. Many patients also feel more tired than usual.
warnings: This medicine can seriously lower your blood cell counts, especially white blood cells, which fight infection — call your doctor right away if you have a fever, chills, or signs of infection. It can cause nerve damage (numbness, tingling, or pain in hands and feet) that may last after treatment. Tell your doctor if you have heart rhythm problems (QT prolongation), liver or kidney disease, or if you are pregnant or breastfeeding, as eribulin can harm an unborn baby. Regular blood tests are needed to monitor your counts during treatment.
typical_dosing: Eribulin is given as an intravenous (IV) infusion directly into a vein, usually over about 2 to 5 minutes. The typical schedule is one dose on Day 1 and one dose on Day 8 of a 21-day cycle, then a rest period before the next cycle. Your doctor may adjust your dose based on how your body responds and your blood test results.
